sections.html:
Grand Forks County spreads over 1,439 square miles along North Dakota's eastern border, where the Red River marks the line with Minnesota. Its seat and biggest community is the city of Grand Forks. Residents numbered 73,170 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 74,501 ranks third in the state.

Beyond Grand Forks itself, the county is made of farm townships and small towns such as Larimore, Northwood and Thompson. Your school district line depends on the parcel's location, since Grand Forks, Thompson, Larimore and Northwood each cover part of the county. East Grand Forks belongs to the same metro area but is across the river in Minnesota, under different state and county rules.

Expect to deal with three county offices. Tax Equalization works with township and city assessors on values. The Treasurer sends bills and takes money. The Recorder files ownership documents. Tax Equalization and the Recorder are both found at 151 South 4th Street, Grand Forks, ND 58201.

  • Tax Equalization Office: uniform assessment, mobile home permits and statements. Call 701-780-8259 (director). Mail to PO Box 5294, Grand Forks ND 58206-5294.
  • County Treasurer: real estate tax bills and payments. Phone 701-780-8292. Write to PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638.
  • Recorder: files deeds and other title documents. Phone 701-780-8262. Write to PO Box 5066.

Who values the parcel depends on where it is. Urban parcels go to the City of Grand Forks Assessing Department. Rural and small town parcels are handled by township and city assessors reporting to the county. Mobile homes are processed by Tax Equalization. Farmland is valued by a separate state method, so check with the office about which category fits yours.

Direct lines also exist for a Real Estate Assessor at 701-780-8245 and a Real Estate Tax Assistant at 701-780-8251. Extensions can change, so confirm when you call.

sections.h2: Due dates and the yearly calendar
sections.html:
The bill is dated January 1 and carries no penalty through March 1. A full-year payment made by February 15 takes 5 percent off. Under state law, statements must be postmarked by December 26. Owners who split the year pay the first installment March 1 and the second October 15.

StepDate
Valuation dateFebruary 1
City or township board of equalizationFirst 15 days of April
County board of equalizationFirst 10 days of June
State board of equalizationSecond Tuesday of August
Budget notices from the treasurerAugust 31
Statements postmarkedBy December 26
5% discount deadlineFebruary 15
Abatement applicationNovember 1 of the next year

Century Code section 57-20-01 adds a 3 percent penalty after March 1, then another on May 1, July 1 and October 15. Second-half payments pick up 6 percent after October 15.

Several free web tools cover county and city property alike. Vanguard house information pages carry valuation detail. The Tyler iTax site carries real estate and mobile home tax records. An ArcGIS map shows parcel lines, and iDoc holds recorded documents.

  • iTax: today's balance, searched by address, owner name or property number
  • Vanguard: how the parcel was valued
  • iDoc: deeds and other filings, searched by grantor and grantee

Treat the maps as a reference only, since they are no substitute for a legal description. Order a survey or title search if a boundary affects your sale.

Begin with a conversation with your parcel's assessor. Next comes the local board's April meeting and the county board's June meeting. The state board will lower a value only if you took your appeal through both of those.

A written notice tells each owner the true and full value for this year and last year. Once the August state meeting is over, abatement of the current assessment can still be requested until November 1 of the year after the tax is payable. The State Tax Commissioner's website has the forms.

Owners inside Grand Forks use the city board. For that board, an appeal by letter, phone or electronic message is treated the same as showing up.

Tax left unpaid turns into a lien on the parcel. When it stays delinquent into a third year, the county can foreclose. Notice is served by June 1, and paying every tax, special, interest charge, penalty and cost by October 1 stops the foreclosure.

Each year the county site publishes its Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien. Once the county holds a tax deed, a former owner can still repurchase ahead of any resale, with the commissioners' approval.

Because the tax lien ranks first, a tax foreclosure can erase a mortgage. Lenders know this, and loan servicers often pay the tax themselves on non-escrow loans and then add that amount to the balance.

At closing, the unpaid balance comes out of your proceeds, and then the Recorder files the new deed. No deed or mortgage tax exists in North Dakota, so the only cost at that step is a recording fee. For copies, the Recorder charges $1.00 a page, plus $5.00 for the first page of a certified copy.

Inherited the house, or fell behind? Do these things before you list:

  • Ask the Treasurer for the full payoff.
  • Ask the city or township about specials.
  • Search the parcel on iTax to confirm the balance matches your records.
  • Check whether a foreclosure notice has been posted for the parcel.

A cash sale can close without a buyer's lender and appraisal, which removes one cause of delay when a foreclosure date is near. We buy Grand Forks County houses in any condition and coordinate with the title company, so the county balance is paid at closing.

sections.h2: A sale from start to finish
sections.html:
Selling a Grand Forks County house has the same basic order whether you list or take a cash offer. First comes the balance check: the Treasurer's payoff for the real estate tax, and a call to the city or township about any specials. Next the buyer's side orders title work, and any liens show up there. At closing the title company pays the county from your proceeds, you sign the deed, and the Recorder files it.

Two dates can force the pace. One is the February 15 discount deadline, which only matters if you are still the owner when the bill is due. The other is the October 1 foreclosure date for parcels in their third delinquent year. If you are close to either one, say so up front so the buyer and the title company can plan around it.

Bring a few papers to the first conversation: your latest tax statement, any notice from the Treasurer, your mortgage payoff letter if there is a loan, and the deed or estate paperwork if you inherited. With those in hand the title company can usually give you a clear net figure quickly.

A cash buyer does not need a lender's appraisal or loan approval. That removes the waiting period that often delays a closing, and it means the buyer's financing cannot fall through. The house is bought as it stands, so you do not schedule repairs, staging or showings.

The county side does not change. The tax balance, specials and any recorded liens still get paid at closing, and the Recorder still files the deed. What changes is the timeline and how many people have to approve the deal before it closes.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Grand Forks County Treasurer?
faqs.a: Call 701-780-8292 or write to PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638.

faqs.q: Who sets the value of a Grand Forks County home?
faqs.a: Outside city limits, the Tax Equalization Office does so with township and city assessors. Inside Grand Forks, the city's own Assessing Department handles it.

faqs.q: What is the early payment deadline?
faqs.a: February 15. A full-year payment by that day knocks off 5 percent. Otherwise the first half is due March 1.

faqs.q: Where can I see my balance online?
faqs.a: The county's Tyler iTax site searches by address, owner name or property number. Vanguard pages show how the property was valued.

faqs.q: Can a former owner buy a property back after tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: Possibly. State law allows repurchase before the county resells, either in one payment or through an installment contract with the commissioners.
